title: Why your inflation isn't the official number
tension: When the news says inflation is 5 percent, almost no one is actually experiencing 5 percent. The official figure is an average of a single fixed basket meant to stand for a 'representative' Indian who does not exist: it blends the villager and the metro renter, the family that spends half its money on food and the one that spends it on school fees and EMIs. The number is true and useless at once, true as a national average, useless as a description of your month. Your real inflation depends on who and where you are.
teachingGoal: Show why the gap between official and felt inflation is real and explainable, not a conspiracy: the index is an average of a fixed basket that differs from any individual's; rural and urban Indians face different inflation; the poor and the rich feel different inflation because their baskets differ; and personal inflation can run higher because of rent, fees, healthcare or fuel. The reader should learn to read inflation as if it is about them.
sectionArc: Why does the official number feel wrong? (it is a weighted average of a fixed, representative basket; your basket is not the representative one)
Whose basket is it, anyway? (the CPI basket weights; the 'average household' it is built around, and why almost no real household matches it)
Rural and urban: two different inflations (separate rural and urban CPI; today's rural versus urban rates, headline and food; why they differ)

And it is not just village versus city: even two states can feel opposite inflations at the same moment. In late 2025, Kerala's retail inflation ran near 9.5% while Telangana's was under 2% and the all-India figure was about 1.3%; show this spread and explain why states diverge (local food and supply, the weight of gold and services, remittance-driven demand)
Why the poor and the rich feel different inflation (the poor's basket is food-heavy, so food inflation is largely their inflation; the better-off feel services, rent and fees more; Engel's law again)
Why your personal inflation can run higher than the headline (rent, school fees, healthcare, fuel if you commute; items you buy more of, or that are underweighted for you)
So is the official number wrong? (no, it is a faithful average, but an average hides the spread, and a fixed basket lags how people actually spend now)
How to read inflation as if it is about you (identify your big-ticket items, weight them yourself; if you are poorer, watch food; if you are urban, watch rent and services)
mustTeach: official CPI is a weighted average of a fixed basket built around a 'representative' household that few people match
India publishes separate rural and urban CPI, and the two differ
the poor face a more food-heavy inflation; the better-off feel services, rent and fees more (Engel's law)
personal inflation can exceed the headline because of items you buy more of or that are underweighted for you
the official number is a faithful average, but an average hides the spread and a fixed basket lags real spending

CURRENCY (important): the current official basket is the 2024-base series, launched 12 Feb 2026. Use the 2024 weights (food and beverages 36.75%) as the CURRENT weights, and cite the old 2012 weights only to show what changed. The detailed month-by-month component inflation figures (vegetables, onion, etc.) come from the longer 2012-base series and must be framed as recent readings under the previous basket, never invented for the new base.
inflation differs sharply across states at the same moment (e.g. Kerala far above the all-India figure while Telangana sits near it), not just between rural and urban

contextCards.fact: Engel's law: poorer households spend a larger share of their income on food. So a single inflation basket cannot fit everyone: for a poor family, where food may be most of the budget, food inflation is close to their true inflation, while for a richer, urban household, rent, school fees, healthcare and transport matter far more. The official index averages across all of them and matches none exactly.

On 12 February 2026 India launched a new Consumer Price Index series with base year 2024 (replacing 2012), built on the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey of 2023-24. The biggest change: the weight of food and beverages fell from 45.86% to 36.75%, because Indians now spend a smaller share of their budgets on food and more on services, a textbook case of Engel's law. Housing and utilities rose to about 17.7%, transport and communication to about 12.4%, and health to about 6.1%. The basket grew from 299 to 358 items, adding e-commerce and online prices, telecom data plans and OTT streaming subscriptions for the first time, and switched to the international COICOP classification of 12 divisions instead of the old six groups. Headline inflation on the new base was 2.75% in January 2026.
contextCards.source: MoSPI / NSO, first CPI release on base 2024=100, 12 February 2026; HCES 2023-24

contextCards.fact: Inflation is far from uniform across India. State-level CPI data shows wide gaps at the very same time: in December 2025, Kerala's retail inflation ran around 9.5% while Telangana's was about 1.8% and the all-India headline was about 1.3%. States diverge because their consumption baskets, local food and supply conditions, and exposure to things like gold, services and remittance-driven demand all differ. Kerala has long been among the higher-inflation states.
contextCards.source: MoSPI eSankhyiki, state-level CPI (General, Combined, 2012=100), December 2025
